title: What a Paycheck Really Looked Like in 1962 America

scenes.text: It's Friday afternoon in nineteen sixty-two. Your husband comes through the front door, hangs his hat on the hook, and puts an envelope on the kitchen table. Or maybe it's your own envelope, from the bank or the store where you work. Either way, everybody in the house knows what Friday means. Payday.
scenes.caption: FRIDAY, 1962

scenes.text: Tonight we're going to follow that one paycheck. Where it came from, how big it was, and exactly where every dollar went. The rent or the mortgage. The groceries. The car. The doctor. The church plate. And the little bit left over at the end, if there was any.
scenes.caption: FOLLOW ONE PAYCHECK

scenes.text: Because the numbers from nineteen sixty-two tell a story that might surprise you. Some things cost almost nothing. Some things cost a great deal more than you'd think. And one paycheck, for a lot of American families, was enough to carry the whole household. Let's open the envelope.
scenes.caption: OPEN THE ENVELOPE

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty-two, the median family income in America was a little under six thousand dollars a year. That works out to roughly one hundred and fifteen dollars a week, before taxes. In most of those families, it was mostly one paycheck, earned by the father, while the mother ran the house.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $115 A WEEK
scenes.chapter: How much was in the envelope

scenes.text: A factory worker with a union job might take home around two and a half dollars an hour. A schoolteacher earned around five thousand dollars a year. A young woman in an office might earn sixty or seventy dollars a week. And the federal minimum wage, for the jobs at the bottom, was one dollar and fifteen cents an hour.
scenes.caption: $1.15 AN HOUR MINIMUM

scenes.text: Taxes came out first. Federal income tax, and Social Security, which in nineteen sixty-two took three and one-eighth percent of your pay, up to a limit. Many states took a bit more. What was left went home in the envelope, or more and more often now, as a paper check you took to the bank on Saturday morning.
scenes.caption: WHAT CAME OUT FIRST

scenes.text: At the bank, you stood in line with your passbook. The teller wrote your deposit in by hand, stamped it, and slid it back across the marble counter. Some of the money went into checking, for the bills. And if you were careful, a few dollars went into savings, where it earned a little interest every quarter.
scenes.caption: THE PASSBOOK

scenes.text: For the man of the house, the paycheck said something about who he was. Bringing home enough to support a wife and children on one income was a point of pride in nineteen sixty-two. Men compared notes quietly at the barber shop and the bowling alley, and a raise of five dollars a week was news worth sharing at the dinner table.
scenes.caption: A POINT OF PRIDE

scenes.text: The biggest bill was the house. In the early sixties, the typical new house sold for around eighteen thousand dollars. With a thirty-year mortgage, often backed by the government for veterans, the monthly payment might be around one hundred dollars, including taxes and insurance.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $18,000 FOR A HOUSE

scenes.text: That meant about a quarter of the paycheck went to the house. The rule of thumb, which every banker repeated, was that a family should never spend more than one week's pay out of every month on housing. In nineteen sixty-two, most families could actually follow it.
scenes.caption: ONE WEEK'S PAY

scenes.text: Renters in the city might pay seventy or eighty dollars a month for an apartment. The landlord often lived in the same building, collected the rent in person on the first of the month, and wrote you a receipt in a little book. Heat and hot water were usually included.
scenes.caption: RENT DAY

scenes.text: Then there were the utilities. The electric bill, the gas bill, the water bill and the telephone, which was rented from the telephone company, not owned. Together, they might run around twenty or twenty-five dollars a month. Long-distance calls were the dangerous part, and every family had a rule about them.
scenes.caption: THE TELEPHONE BILL

scenes.text: Heating the house was its own expense. Many homes still burned fuel oil, delivered by a truck that filled a tank in the basement. Some older houses still had coal furnaces. And in winter, the rule in a great many homes was simple. If you're cold, put on a sweater, and don't touch that thermostat.
scenes.caption: PUT ON A SWEATER

scenes.text: Next came the groceries. A family of four might spend around twenty to twenty-five dollars a week at the supermarket. That was nearly a fifth of the paycheck, a much bigger share than families spend today. Food was the second biggest bill in almost every house.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $25 A WEEK

scenes.text: Here's what that money bought. A loaf of white bread for around twenty cents. A dozen eggs for around thirty cents. A pound of ground beef for around fifty cents. A half-gallon of milk delivered to your door, or bought at the store, for around fifty cents. Coffee came in a can, and nobody had heard of spending a dollar on a single cup.
scenes.caption: BREAD FOR 20 CENTS

scenes.text: Mothers stretched every dollar. They clipped coupons from the newspaper. They saved trading stamps from the supermarket, licked them into little books, and traded the books for a toaster or a lamp. They bought a whole chicken and made it last three nights. Nothing was ever thrown away.
scenes.caption: STRETCHING EVERY DOLLAR

scenes.text: A lot of families also grew part of their own food. A vegetable garden behind the house, tomatoes and beans and squash in the summer, and jars of canned peaches and pickles lined up on basement shelves for the winter. In small towns, some families still kept chickens in the backyard for eggs.
scenes.caption: THE BACKYARD GARDEN

scenes.text: The milkman still came to many neighborhoods two or three times a week, leaving glass bottles on the front step in a little metal box. The bread man came too, in some towns, and the egg man from the farm outside town. You paid them weekly, in cash, or they kept a running tab in a little notebook.
scenes.caption: THE MILKMAN'S NOTEBOOK

scenes.text: A dinner out was a real treat. A family might go to a diner or a cafeteria once a month, where a hamburger cost around thirty or forty cents. And the new fast-food stands along the highway, with their golden signs, sold a hamburger for fifteen cents, which seemed almost too good to be true.
scenes.caption: DINNER OUT

scenes.text: After the house and the food came the car. A brand-new Chevrolet or Ford cost somewhere around two thousand five hundred dollars. Most families bought it on time, with a loan, and paid around sixty or seventy dollars a month for three years. A lot of families bought a good used car instead.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $2,500 FOR A NEW CAR

scenes.text: Gasoline cost around thirty cents a gallon, and the man at the station pumped it for you. A family car might get twelve or fifteen miles per gallon, and nobody worried much about it. A Sunday drive to see the grandparents might cost a dollar in gas, there and back.
scenes.caption: 30 CENTS A GALLON

scenes.text: The car was expensive to keep up, though. Tires wore out quickly. The oil was changed every thousand miles. And every few years, the family car needed a new muffler, a new battery, or a whole new transmission, which could eat a month's savings in one afternoon.
scenes.caption: THE REPAIR BILL

scenes.text: Car insurance was cheaper than today but still a real bill, and many families paid it twice a year. Most people didn't carry much coverage. And plenty of fathers did their own repairs on Saturday mornings, with the hood up in the driveway and a son handing him the wrenches one at a time.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY IN THE DRIVEWAY

scenes.text: Then came all the smaller things. Clothing, much of it sewn at home or handed down from older brothers and sisters. A visit to the doctor, which might cost five dollars, paid in cash at the front desk. The family dentist. Haircuts. Shoes resoled at the cobbler instead of thrown away.
scenes.caption: SEWN AT HOME

scenes.text: A first-class stamp cost four cents, until it went up to five cents in January of nineteen sixty-three. The newspaper cost a dime. A movie ticket cost well under a dollar. And a family could spend a whole Saturday at the county fair for a few dollars, including the cotton candy.
scenes.caption: A FOUR-CENT STAMP

scenes.text: There was the collection plate on Sunday, which many families took seriously, and often a weekly envelope with the family's name on it. There were the insurance payments, to a man who sometimes came right to the door to collect them. And there was the Christmas club at the bank, a dollar or two a week saved all year for presents in December.
scenes.caption: THE CHRISTMAS CLUB

scenes.text: And there was credit, though not as much as today. Department stores gave charge accounts to good customers. A few people carried a new kind of card from a company called Diners Club. But most families still paid cash, and if they couldn't afford something, they waited until they could.
scenes.caption: PAY CASH OR WAIT

scenes.text: Some families bought big things on the installment plan. A new refrigerator, a washing machine, or a console television might be paid off at a few dollars a month for two years. A payment book came with it, a little booklet of coupons, one torn out and mailed in with a check every month until the last one was gone.
scenes.caption: THE PAYMENT BOOK

scenes.text: And what about vacations? For many families, the summer vacation was a week at a lake cabin, a trip to see relatives, or a long drive to a national park, with the whole family packed into the station wagon. Motels cost around eight or ten dollars a night. Mother packed sandwiches so nobody had to pay for lunch on the road.
scenes.caption: THE SUMMER VACATION

scenes.text: So how did families keep it all straight? In a lot of houses, the answer was the envelope system. On payday, the mother sat at the kitchen table and divided the cash into envelopes. One for the house. One for groceries. One for the car. One for church. One for the doctor. One for savings, if there was anything left.
scenes.caption: THE ENVELOPE SYSTEM

scenes.text: When the grocery envelope was empty, the grocery shopping was done until next Friday. That was the whole budget, right there in a shoebox or a kitchen drawer. No spreadsheets. No apps. Just a pencil, a stack of envelopes, and a woman who knew exactly where every dollar went.
scenes.caption: WHEN IT'S GONE, IT'S GONE

scenes.text: Many fathers handed the whole envelope to their wives and received a small allowance back, for lunch, gas and the barber. It sounds strange now. But in nineteen sixty-two, in a great many American homes, the person who actually managed the money was the mother.
scenes.caption: MOTHER KEPT THE BOOKS

scenes.text: Was it easier back then? In some ways, yes. One paycheck could buy a house, a car, and three meals a day for a family of four or five. Housing took about a quarter of the pay. A young couple with a high school education could often afford a home of their own before thirty.
scenes.caption: ONE PAYCHECK WAS ENOUGH

scenes.text: In other ways, no. Families had far less. One car. One television. One bathroom, for six people. Clothes were mended until they fell apart. A long-distance call was an event. And many Americans, especially in the rural South, in the cities and in minority neighborhoods, never got anywhere near that median paycheck at all.
scenes.caption: BUT THEY HAD LESS

scenes.text: What's certain is this. People knew the value of a dollar, because they could see it, hold it, and count it out on the kitchen table every Friday. That habit stayed with that generation for the rest of their lives. If your parents or grandparents saved string and rubber bands, now you know why.
scenes.caption: THE VALUE OF A DOLLAR

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What did your father or mother earn in the sixties, and what did your family's house cost? We read every one. And stay with us for more. Next time, we'll take you to the main streets of small-town America, in full color. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOUR HOUSE COST?
